explainedBy: The writer holds out his pages and the busy reader walks straight past: nobody wants to read it.

storyboard.claim: Nobody wants to read your writing; believing that makes you write things people cannot put down.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The aspiring writer reaching out with his pages while the red-coated reader walks past, blank-faced.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opening claim.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the rejection as an event: offered pages, a reader who keeps walking.

explainedBy: Cause and effect: accepting the ego death leads to liberation.

storyboard.claim: It is the ultimate ego death for a creator, but internalized it becomes liberation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A two-step flow: Ego death -> Liberation.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names what accepting the opening claim costs and gives.
storyboard.addedInformation: The flow shows the turn from loss to freedom as a sequence.

explainedBy: The author himself holding his blunt book: this is whose idea we are unpacking.

storyboard.claim: The hosts are unpacking Steven Pressfield's incredibly blunt book.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Veteran Pressfield holding up his book with a wry smirk.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the quote to its author.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the author and the book as an object.

callout.text: how you look at a blank page

explainedBy: The aspiring writer sitting before the typewriter and its blank sheet: the lens changes how he sees the blank page.

storyboard.claim: The lens of the book will change how you look at a blank page.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The aspiring writer seated, uneasy, beside a typewriter with an empty sheet.
storyboard.onScreenText: how you look at a blank page
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the book to the viewer at his own desk.
storyboard.addedInformation: Puts the blank page and the writer facing it on screen.

explainedBy: The writer offers his page and the reader faces him as an opponent, not an audience.

storyboard.claim: The reader is not your audience; the reader is your adversary, on every page and paragraph.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The writer holding out his page to the reader, who glares back at him.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the writer-and-reader pair, now as opponents.
storyboard.addedInformation: The angry partner face turns the reader into an adversary.

explainedBy: Every sentence is a negotiation: the writer pitches with an eager smile while the reader is already walking off, looking for a reason to stop.

storyboard.claim: Every sentence is a negotiation with someone desperately looking for a reason to stop reading.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The writer talking eagerly with his page while the reader turns away and walks.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same pair: the reader stops glaring and starts leaving; the writer pleads.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the negotiation and the reader’s readiness to quit.

explainedBy: The mission as a change: from begging for scattered attention to structurally earning it.

storyboard.claim: In a hostile environment the mission is to stop begging for attention and start structurally earning it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: Begging -> Earning.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the problem to the goal of the deep dive.
storyboard.addedInformation: States the shift the whole video is about.

explainedBy: A teacher lecturing in a classroom: the standard creative-writing advice the thesis goes against.

storyboard.claim: The thesis goes against what you hear in a high school creative writing class or a poetry seminar.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A teacher at the front of a classroom, cheerfully lecturing.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Introduces the conventional advice being challenged.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the usual advice in the classroom where it is taught.

explainedBy: The student follows the advice: he pours his soul on the page and celebrates, expecting the world to resonate.

storyboard.claim: Most advice says find your voice, express your truth, and the world will resonate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The aspiring writer celebrating with his pages in the classroom.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the teacher to the student acting on the advice.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the hopeful self-expression the book will reject.

explainedBy: Pressfield points at the self-expressing writer and calls self-expression the problem; the writer is caught off guard.

storyboard.claim: Pressfield argues the opposite: self-expression is the actual problem.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pressfield pointing at the surprised writer; the word Self-expression struck through.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Pressfield answers the advice of the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike and the surprised writer show the advice being rejected.

explainedBy: The writer's job as a mechanism: empathy turned into structure.

storyboard.claim: The writer's real job is empathy turned into structure.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: Empathy -> Structure.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Replaces self-expression with the book’s formula.
storyboard.addedInformation: The core thesis as a two-step mechanism.

explainedBy: The parts of that structure: the hook, the build, the payoff.

storyboard.claim: Structure is the hook, the build, the payoff, a clear concept, a theme, a villain.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A three-step flow: Hook -> Build -> Payoff.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Spells out what structure is made of.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the order of the main structural tools.

explainedBy: One blueprint, many forms: the same structure sorts across a dog food ad, a blockbuster and a literary novel.

storyboard.claim: The same structural blueprint holds for a dog food ad, a Hollywood blockbuster, a literary novel.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter with three buckets: Dog food ad, Hollywood blockbuster, Literary novel.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Applies the structure to forms of writing.
storyboard.addedInformation: Lists the forms the blueprint covers.

explainedBy: The list completes with the self-help book: the blueprint is universal because the human mind is.

storyboard.claim: ...or a self-help book; it shows how universal the human mind is at processing information.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same sorter gains a fourth bucket: Self-help book.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same sorter, one more bucket.
storyboard.addedInformation: Completes the range of forms.

explainedBy: Against the mist of inspiration, Pressfield points to a built bridge: art is architecture.

storyboard.claim: We want art to be an unstructured mist of inspiration; Pressfield says no, it is architecture.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pressfield pointing at a suspension bridge.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the forms to what they share.
storyboard.addedInformation: A built structure stands for writing as construction.

explainedBy: The bridge stays: writing is engineering, a craft he learned outside the ivory tower.

storyboard.claim: It's engineering, and he did not learn it in an ivory-tower MFA program.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Pressfield now talking beside the same bridge, wry.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same bridge; architecture becomes engineering.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the MFA contrast is carried by the words only.

explainedBy: The young Pressfield in his 1960s suit walking to work: the bottom of the creative food chain, 1967.

storyboard.claim: He started at the bottom of the creative food chain; the year is 1967.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Young Pressfield in a narrow charcoal suit walking with a briefcase.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Cuts back to where Pressfield began.
storyboard.addedInformation: Introduces the young Pressfield and the era.

explainedBy: He arrives at a New York tower, 666 Fifth Avenue.

storyboard.claim: Picture the Tishman building, 666 Fifth Avenue, New York; we are in the elevator.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The city skyline appears behind the walking young Pressfield.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same walk; the city appears.
storyboard.addedInformation: Places the scene in New York.

explainedBy: The 23-year-old junior copywriter with his typewriter and his small pay: $150 a week.

storyboard.claim: A 23-year-old Pressfield makes $150 a week as a junior copywriter at Benton & Bowles.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Young Pressfield in the agency office holding his pay beside a typewriter.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the street into the agency.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the job (typewriter) and the low pay.

explainedBy: He rides up, wide-eyed, watching the floors ding by.
noVisual: No elevator or floor panel in the vocabulary; the ride is carried by the callout and his face.

storyboard.claim: He rides the elevator up through the smoke, watching the lighted floor panel.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Young Pressfield wide-eyed, hands free.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same office; the coin is put away, his face lights up.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the elevator itself cannot be drawn.

explainedBy: The building as floors: media on 14, account management on 17.

storyboard.claim: Floor 14 is media, floor 17 is account management, but his floor is 16.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A sorter listing Floor 14: Media and Floor 17: Accounts.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Shows the floors he passes.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the muted viewer the floor directory.

explainedBy: He steps off at the creative department and celebrates: he has made it.

storyboard.claim: The brass panel says creative department; he steps off feeling he has made it.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Young Pressfield celebrating in the office.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Floor 16 revealed after 14 and 17.
storyboard.addedInformation: His triumph is on his body.

explainedBy: The same young man slumps: the reality of the job is that nobody cares.

storyboard.claim: He feels like a capital-C creative, then the icy reality hits: nobody cares.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The celebrating young Pressfield slumps, sad.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same man: triumph turns to deflation.
storyboard.addedInformation: The change of body shows the reality hitting.

explainedBy: A teacher reading a student paper because it is her job: she is paid to read it.

storyboard.claim: In the classroom your teachers are literally paid a salary to read your work.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A professor holding a student paper.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the agency to how we are conditioned at school.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the artificial reader who has to read.

explainedBy: She grades it out of duty, blank-faced; that artificial reader breeds the delusion that the world is waiting.

storyboard.claim: They have to read your dissertation to grade it, so you believe the world is waiting for your words.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The same professor now reads with a blank face; the delusion is struck through.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same teacher: her face turns to duty.
storyboard.addedInformation: The strike marks the belief as a delusion.

explainedBy: A TV commercial plays and the reader walks away from it, annoyed: people hate ads.

storyboard.claim: In the real world your copy is invisible; people despise ads and hate TV commercials.
storyboard.concreteVisual: An old TV showing a commercial while the reader walks away angrily.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the classroom to the real world.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the hostility to ads as an act of walking away.

explainedBy: Degrees: you do not start at zero with a reader, you start far below it.

storyboard.claim: They hate your writing sight unseen, so you start not at zero but at a massive deficit.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A spectrum from Massive deficit to Zero with the marker at the deficit end.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Draws the consequence of the hostility.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows where the writer starts.

explainedBy: The reader holds out her limited time to the writer: reading is a transaction she pays into.

storyboard.claim: You are an annoyance until proven otherwise; reading is a transaction where the reader donates time and attention.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader holding an hourglass, facing the uneasy writer.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the deficit to what the reader gives.
storyboard.addedInformation: The hourglass makes her limited time a held object.

explainedBy: The exchange: the reader gives time and attention, the writer must give something worthy in return.

storyboard.claim: The writer has to give something profoundly worthy in return; that is structural compassion.
storyboard.concreteVisual: A flow: Their time -> Something worthy.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Completes the transaction begun on the previous beat.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows both sides of the exchange.

explainedBy: The copywriter facing his commercial realizes the customer could not care less about it.

storyboard.claim: When you realize the customer could not care less about your 30-second commercial, your mind concentrates.
storyboard.concreteVisual: Young Pressfield slumping beside the TV showing his commercial.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Back to the agency, with his own ad.
storyboard.addedInformation: Ties the lesson to his own work.

explainedBy: He switches to the consumer’s point of view: the reader now stands by the TV and he asks whether it is fun for her.

storyboard.claim: You switch to the point of view of the consumer and ask: is this actually fun?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader joins him at the TV; he points at the ad as she watches blankly.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same TV; the consumer enters the frame.
storyboard.addedInformation: The second person shows the switch of point of view.

callout.text: Am I just talking about myself?

explainedBy: The reader starts to walk away from the ad as he wonders if he is only talking about himself.

storyboard.claim: Is this sexy, informative, or am I just talking about myself? Then the devil’s advocate.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader walks off from the TV while young Pressfield slumps.
storyboard.onScreenText: Am I just talking about myself?
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same TV: the reader leaves, he deflates.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the cost of self-centered copy.

explainedBy: Today’s writer with his thread on his phone, worried that assuming hostility kills his confidence.

storyboard.claim: Doesn't assuming the reader hates your work destroy confidence, say for a newsletter or social media thread?
storyboard.concreteVisual: The aspiring writer at his desk holding his phone, worried.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Devil’s advocate brings the idea to a modern writer.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows who the objection is about.

callout.text: Everyone is going to despise this

explainedBy: He imagines everyone despising it, and fear takes over.

storyboard.claim: If I sat down thinking everyone is going to despise this sight unseen...
storyboard.concreteVisual: Same writer, his face now afraid.
storyboard.onScreenText: Everyone is going to despise this
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same writer: worry becomes fear.
storyboard.addedInformation: The face turns the objection into fear.

explainedBy: He slumps, phone down, unable to type a word: paralyzed.

storyboard.claim: I would be completely paralyzed; it sounds like a firing squad, but it is actually the opposite.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The writer slumps, the phone gone from his hand.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same writer: he gives up holding the phone.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the paralysis in the body.

explainedBy: The reader hurries by on her phone: she is not cruel, just busy.

storyboard.claim: It is freeing once accepted: people are not cruel, just overwhelmingly busy; the most useful humiliation.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The red-coated reader rushing along the street, eyes on her phone.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Answers the fear: the reader is busy, not hostile.
storyboard.addedInformation: Reframes the adversary as hurried.

explainedBy: The beaming ad-agency client, the man who carries client’s disease.

storyboard.claim: The humiliation cures a delusion ad agencies call client's disease.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The stout client in a green plaid suit talking happily.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Names the delusion and who has it.
storyboard.addedInformation: Gives the delusion a face.

callout.text: In love with his own product

explainedBy: The client celebrates beside a heart: he is in love with his own product.

storyboard.claim: Client's disease: thinking anyone cares about your product because you do; the client is in love with his undergarments.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The client celebrating as a heart appears.
storyboard.onScreenText: In love with his own product
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same client; the heart appears.
storyboard.addedInformation: The heart shows the love for the product.

explainedBy: The client raves about stitching and fabric while the ad man beside him looks on blank: nobody else cares.

storyboard.claim: He knows the stitching and fabric and thinks it is the greatest invention, but nobody else cares.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The client talking happily; the veteran ad man enters, blank-faced.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same client and heart; an indifferent listener enters.
storyboard.addedInformation: The blank partner face shows the indifference.

explainedBy: The pro copywriter points to a bridge that reaches the busy, distracted person hurrying past.

storyboard.claim: The pro copywriter knows nobody cares; strip away the ego and build a bridge to the busy, distracted person.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The veteran ad man pointing at a suspension bridge while the reader hurries by.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: From the client’s ego to the copywriter’s answer.
storyboard.addedInformation: The bridge and the passing reader show who it must reach.

explainedBy: The reader stops and takes the gift the writer offers: the experience rewards her for stopping.

storyboard.claim: It is not self-flagellation: put yourself in their shoes and design an experience that rewards them for stopping.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader picks up a gift from the writer on the cue and smiles.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: The busy reader finally stops.
storyboard.addedInformation: Shows the reward as a deed.

explainedBy: She keeps the gift while the writer talks to her in her terms: passion translated into their language.

storyboard.claim: It is about translating your passion into their language; ego death is the prerequisite.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The reader holding the gift as the writer talks to her.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Same pair; the writer now speaks to her.
storyboard.addedInformation: weak: the translation itself is carried by the words.

explainedBy: Back to the formula: empathy turned into structure.

storyboard.claim: It all comes back to empathy turned into structure, which clears the board.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The flow Empathy -> Structure again.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Returns to the thesis of beat 10.
storyboard.addedInformation: Closes the opening argument.

explainedBy: The veteran ad man holds up the lightbulb: the first tool to earn attention is the concept, the big idea.

storyboard.claim: With self-indulgence swept away, the first mechanical tool for earning attention is the concept.
storyboard.concreteVisual: The veteran ad man holding a lightbulb.
storyboard.relationToPrevious: Opens the next section.
storyboard.addedInformation: The lightbulb names the concept as an idea.
